children: The recent pace of earnings growth is unsustainable
What goes up is most likely going to come down again.
When it comes to earnings growth rates, it's possible to have too much of a good thing.

That's because soaring growth rates - such as those seen in recent quarters - are more often than not followed by below-average growth rates, and vice versa. We therefore should resist the temptation to extrapolate the blazingly fast earnings growth of recent quarters into the indefinite future.
As the late British economist John Maynard Keynes reminded us, trees do not grow to the sky.

Nevertheless, the temptation to think that way is strong. With the S&P 500's SPX second-quarter earnings season largely over, we now know that the index's earnings per share in the second quarter were close to 50% higher than in last year's second quarter. That high of a growth rate is extremely rare except for when the economy is emerging from a recession, which of course is not the case currently.

Also extraordinary is the four-quarter EPS growth rate through June 30, which is close to 35%. Since 1928, only 8% of quarters have had a higher trailing four-quarter growth rate. The average is 12.7%.
The chart below plots this mean-reverting tendency of earnings growth rates. It provides investors with yet another reason to worry that the stock market is skating on thin ice.

These raw statistics are not the only reason to resist the temptation to extrapolate recent EPS growth rates into the future, however. That's because some idiosyncratic factors contributed to these recent growth rates, making it even less likely they will persist indefinitely.

Several of these factors were enumerated this week by Arun Sundaram, senior vice president for investment strategy at CFRA. In an email to clients, he pointed out that recent earnings have been inflated by, among other things, "massive unrealized mark-to-market gains on equity investments in Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX (SPCX), benefiting Google (GOOG) (GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT) and Tesla (TSLA); sizable tariff refunds benefiting many consumer companies, including Apple (AAPL), Walmart (WMT) and Procter & Gamble (PG); and a surge in energy-sector earnings, driven by higher oil prices (CL00) (BRN00)" caused by the war with Iran.

Notice that, in each case, there are compelling reasons to explicitly avoid extrapolating recent earnings growth rates into the future. Sundaram writes that these factors "will create some meaningful [year-over-year] comparability issues as we move into 2027."

The bottom line? Go ahead and celebrate corporate America's good fortune. But keep your bullishness in check: History suggests that the S&P 500's EPS growth rate over the next 12 months will be markedly lower than what the market has enjoyed in recent quarters.
